source_refs.note: Book p. 17: 1.6.2 text with Figures 1.10 and 1.11

blocks.text: The graph of the logarithmic function \(y = \log_a x\) is constructed using the properties discussed in the above subsections. In particular, the domain \(x > 0\), the vertical asymptote \(x = 0\), the intercept \((1, 0)\), the continuity, the injectivity and the monotonic behaviour depending on the value of \(a\) together determine the shape and position of the curve. Using these features, the graph can be drawn accurately for different values of the base \(a\).
Figure 1.10 shows the graphs of logarithmic functions with bases greater than 1, whereas Figure 1.11 represents the graphs of logarithmic functions with bases between 0 and 1.

blocks.alt: Graphs of y = log x to the bases 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, e and 10 for x from 0 to 22. All rise from left to right, all pass through the point (1, 0), all fall without bound as x approaches 0 from the right, and the curve with the base closest to 1 is the steepest.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.10: logarithmic functions with bases greater than 1 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graphs of y = log x to the bases 0.1, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9 for x from 0 to 32. All fall from left to right, all pass through the point (1, 0), all rise without bound as x approaches 0 from the right, and the curve with the base closest to 1 (0.9) falls fastest.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.11: logarithmic functions with bases between 0 and 1 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read the two figures:
1. Every curve passes through \((1, 0)\) and stays to the right of the \(y\)-axis, which is the vertical asymptote.
2. Figure 1.10 (\(a > 1\)): every curve rises. For \(x > 1\) the curve with the base closest to 1 is the highest: at \(x = 22\), \(\log_{1.3} x \approx 11.8\) but \(\log_{10} x \approx 1.34\).
3. Figure 1.11 (\(0 < a < 1\)): every curve falls. Again the base closest to 1 (here 0.9) moves fastest: at \(x = 30\), \(\log_{0.9} x \approx -32.3\) (far below the window) but \(\log_{0.1} x \approx -1.48\).
4. The two families are mirror images in the \(x\)-axis: \(\log_{1/a} x = -\log_a x\). For example \(\log_{0.5} x = -\log_2 x\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Sketching \(y = \log_a x\) by hand (our method, using the properties above):
1. Draw the asymptote \(x = 0\) and mark \((1, 0)\).
2. Mark \((a, 1)\) and \((\frac{1}{a}, -1)\), since \(\log_a a = 1\) and \(\log_a \frac{1}{a} = -1\).
3. For \(a > 1\) join them with a rising curve; for \(0 < a < 1\) with a falling one, bending towards the \(y\)-axis near \(x = 0\).
For \(y = \log_2 x\) (our example) the points are \((\frac{1}{4}, -2)\), \((\frac{1}{2}, -1)\), \((1, 0)\), \((2, 1)\), \((4, 2)\), \((8, 3)\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The graph lies only in \(x > 0\), approaches the \(y\)-axis and passes through \((1, 0)\).
2. \(a > 1\): rising curve, below the \(x\)-axis for \(0 < x < 1\), above it for \(x > 1\).
3. \(0 < a < 1\): falling curve, above the \(x\)-axis for \(0 < x < 1\), below it for \(x > 1\).
4. The closer the base is to 1, the steeper the curve.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Drawing the curve crossing the \(y\)-axis or continuing to \(x < 0\).
2. Drawing it flattening towards a horizontal line: \(\log_a x\) has no horizontal asymptote, it keeps rising (or falling) slowly for ever.
3. Thinking a bigger base gives a steeper curve; for \(a > 1\) it is the opposite.
